subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, section 5 of this bill to establish a Department of Reconstruction states that it shall be the duty of the minister, amongst other things, to formulate' plans for housing and community planning and! to provide for carrying out such plans. In my opinion there is no project for reconstruc-
Department of Reconstruction

on the site in construction of a housing project were cut in half, the annual cost of the housing produced would be reduced by only about ten per cent. If the cost of materials entering into the production of the housing were cut in half, the annual cost would be reduced by only about fifteen per cent. But a reduction in the financial charges, interest and amortization, by half would effect a greater reduction in annual cost than the cutting in half of the cost of both material and labour, and therefore I commend the latter method to the government.
The city of Toronto has had a planning board of experts under the chairmanship of Mr. A. G. Partridge, president of the Goodyear Tire and Rubber company, who have been working for some time on city planning, and they have recently issued a very illuminating second annual report. They are therefore in a position to take immediate advantage of a national post-war construction programme to be assisted by the federal government under terms which I hope will be as generous as those of the United States.
The Ontario government is in a position to cooperate with this plan in consequence of having recently set up a department of planning and development under a separate minister, Mr. Dana Porter. May I add that as housing is intimately connected with health, this department should more properly be placed under the Department of National Health. One third of our population would mean four million in the low income group, and to house these would require at least one million housing units. If these cost, say, $2,000 per unit, it would mean a loan of $2 billion. May I point out that this does not mean a gift of this amount of money, but only that it shall be made available as a loan at a low rate of interest to be recovered later on. There is no expenditure that will bring greater returns in health and happiness than housing.

Section agreed to.
Sections 6 to 8 inclusive agreed to.
On section 9-Orders and regulations.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I think the Prime Minister ought to give the committee a better idea of what is proposed to have done under the enabling sections with regard to regulations. He was not in the house the other day when I protested against power of legislation being vested in a minister under a bill which was to come under the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). I was chastised by the minister becauselMr. Bruce.]

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: It was the aeronautics bill.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I think it was under yours too.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: No. Mine was flawless.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I do not
think so. The practice has grown up under all governments in recent years of legislating under the guise of regulations not only for purely administrative affairs but in executive matters and in others that apply to judicial functions, really establishing in the minister the power to set up policy-a principle that is comparable to what a celebrated Lord Chancellor in England characterized over twenty years ago as the new despotism. I think parliament ought to be jealous about delegating to the government the power to make orders in council on the recommendation of a minister, because usually these are matters of routine, I imagine, so far as the council itself is concerned, providing that the ministers may do thus or so in regard to matters which were never contemplated by the enabling statute. I am trying to state a principle in general terms and I think the Prime Minister will agree with me. Take this section 9 (a). Provision is made to transfer to the minister any powers or duties of a government department or agency whether conferred by statute or otherwise and to provide that such powers or duties shall be exercised or performed concurrently or otherwise by the minister. On its face that is a very innocent looking paragraph. Parliament delegates to one department of government the power to carry on certain functions; but here the powers which were delegated to it, particularly by parliament, are being switched or are capable of being switched by order in council to this new minister. What is contemplated by that? It must be put in there for a purpose. Its purpose does not appear on the face of it. What is envisioned by the authority to make a regulation of that kind?
I have no objection at all to paragraph (c) because on its face it relates purely to administration of the act itself. A government which is promoting a bill cannot think of every little administrative authority that ought to be put into it, and those are the things that can be best handled by order in council. So far as I can recall I have never made any protest against the delegation of powers of that kind. But paragraph (b) provides 'that the minister may set up one or more boards or advisory councils to exercise such functions in connection with the administration of this

Department of Reconstruction
act as may be assigned to them by order or regulation. That is a new thought. We are delegating authority to a minister to do certain things, or to a department of government to do certain things, and in paragraph (b) we are giving authority to the minister, to whom parliament has already delegated powers or authority, to redelegate those powers or authority to some unknown board, governmental agency or department not envisioned by parliament by statute or otherwise. I should like to know what is contemplated by this. It seems to me it is carrying the power of delegation almost to the nth degree. The Prime Minister ought to justify the redelegation, if I may use that term, of such powers as are contemplated by paragraph (b) of section 9. The authority conferred by paragraphs (a) and (b) of section 9 are open to question at least. I am trying to be moderate in what I say about it. Until we have had some further explanation from the Prime Minister I do not think this ought to pass.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: First of all may I say I am sorry I was away when my hon. friend was chastised. Had I been here I would have done the best I could to save him any affliction.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: It did not do any harm; it left no scar.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Let me say at once that practically speaking I agree with him' when he says it is desirable that there should be as little in the way of delegation of important powers as possible, and that it is important that powers should be set forth in the statute rather than given under order in council or by regulation. On the other hand, I think my hon. friend will agree that the business of government to-day has become such that unless there were delegation of power it would be altogether impossible to have it carried on. No minister could begin to discharge the duties that are assigned to him in a statute unless he were given some authority to delegate some of those duties and to bring to his assistance whatever he might need in the way of advisory boards and councils. In debating this matter the other day the leader of the opposition suggested that it would be well for the government to consider the advisability of having some kind of a permanent board set up by the minister which would have on it representatives of the different provinces, and, I think he also added, representatives of the municipalities.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That was for the purpose of reconstruction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Yes, and reconstruction is the subject of the bill with which we are dealing. The section my hon. friend is complaining of, if he is complaining, is the one that is intended to help meet a situation of the kind. Recently the premier of Ontario suggested that there should be a joint board of the dominion and the provinces for certain purposes. Well, that may be a very good suggestion, and it may be desirable to carry it out; but unless there were a clause in the statute which gave the minister the necessary authority to effect that end he would be unable to do so without the passing by parliament of another act. I can assure my hon. friend that this section is not intended to go any farther in the matter of conferring powers on ministers of the crown, or on deputy ministers or boards, than is absolutely essential for effective administration.
I would recall to my hon. friend a statute passed when, if I am not mistaken, he was a member of the ministry. It may have been before he was a member of the ministry, because it was in Sir Robert Borden's time. There was an act passed during that time to authorize the rearrangement and transfers of duties in the public service. That statute gives the power to a minister of the crown by order in council to transfer from one department of government to another department many of the duties assigned, in the first instance, to a particular department. As I read this section, particularly paragraph (a), it really goes no farther than that. The governor in council may make such order or regulation as may be deemed necessary or advisable to transfer to the minister any powers or duties of a government department or agency whether conferred by statute or otherwise and to provide that such powers or duties shall be exercised or performed concurrently or otherwise by the minister. That paragraph may have been unnecessary in view of the powers which are given by statute to authorize the rearrangement and transfer of duties in the public service.
Paragraph (b) reads:
To establish one or more boards or advisory councils to exercise such functions in connection with the administration of this act as may be assigned to them by order or regulation.
That is desirable to enable the minister to get the best advice that he can obtain in dealing with the large questions that will come before him. For example, the minister may wish to have the advice of labour and of industry on a great many matters, just as is
Department of Reconstruction

done to-day in connection with work of the Department of Labour, and beyond question this would' give him that power.
On reflection I think that my hon. friend will see that there is nothing being done under this paragraph that will in any way widen existing authority.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
It is rather reassuring to have the Prime Minister make that statement. I thought that the statement of the general principle which I made would find response in his mind, because I recall on a good many occasions through the long period of time that I have been in the house that he himself has been in the very van in apposing the principle incorporated in this paragraph. It seems to me that it all depends on where you sit in this house as to whether a principle is good or bad. I can quite understand the government desiring to enlarge its powers irrespective of parliament for the purpose of convenience. I am not unimpressed by the statement of the Prime Minister that government is a very comiplex problem at the present time. Speaking generally I think that is the best argument he has. The government could not be running back to parliament every day or two for a new enabling act. The executive must have some authority to meet new situations. When I make that statement of fact I think the Prime Minister will agree that I am very fair-minded about this thing; but I had in mind that from time to time heretofore the government had been allocating departments, branches, bureaux or whatever they may be-I think "government departs ment" is the term mostly used-from one portfolio to another. It has been doing that as long as I can remember, and I know the .power existed long, before I had any connection with parliament.
The Prime Minister has referred to a statute which is still! unrapealed. I wonder if my right hon. friend opposed it at the time it was passed. It would be a matter of historical curiosity to find out what his attitude was in regard to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I am not sure I was in the house when it was passed, though I may have been if it was in the session of 1919-1920.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
That may be so. If my hon. friend was not here I venture to suggest that those who were here did not accept the principle -without scrutiny and examination and a good deal of protest. Generally speaking this power ought to be limited purely to administration; I think we are both in agreement on that.

I am not yet sure that the Prime Minister has made out a case for subsections (a) and Ob). Certainly if subsection (b) means anything at all; if it is anything more than window dressing; if these boards or advisory councils are to have any authority, something more is required, because all they can possibly do under this section is give the minister advice, and he can get that advice without the power to set up a board. He can consult those who are in a position to give him advice on any of the points with respect to which it is suggested that power should be vested in these councils; in fact they have no powers at all, they are merely consultative bodies from which the minister may request advice. My colleague from Yale points out that this power already is conferred by subsection (d) of section 6, so that it would look as .though there were redundancy. Section 6 (d) provides:
The minister, to enable him to perform the duties imposed upon him by this act, may establish committees or boards and use existing organizations and agencies to assist shim in carrying out the purposes of this act.
That would include the right of consultation ; so that it would seem that the draftsman here had gone beyond what was required, or that' something' more is contemplated by section 9 (b) than has been intimated by the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister did make a point with respect to the setting up of joint boards. Inasmuch as the jurisdiction relating to reconstruction is almost entirely a matter of property and civil rights, and therefore within the ambit of the powers of the provinces, I think it would be a. good thing if the jurisdiction and constitutional rights of the provinces were recognized specifically in the bill. With all this talk about rehabilitation and reconstruction I am afraid we are going to see a multiplicity of boards and authorities and powers set up in the country, .all having one good end in view, but with a tremendous overlapping of personnel and of cost to the taxpayer, whether provincially or federally, unless there is some coordinating authority. That, of course, is the distinguishing point of this bill; it is an attempt, and I .think an honest attempt, to arrange for the coordination of these bodies that .are to be set up. Every province will have its own ideas. Only the other day I read with a good deal of interest that the premier of Nova Scotia had given to the public a scheme of reconstruction and rehabilitation for that little province which would cost anywhere from $70,000,000 to $100,000,000. He expects the federal treasury to bear half the cost, and then he wields the big stick and says if they do not bear half the cost he is going to

Department oj Reconstruction
reenter the field of income taxation. I may not be quoting him accurately, but that was the impression left upon my mind. So that there is great need of a reorientation of the whole field, and certainly there is great need of joint operation, joint thought and joint action on the part of the dominion and the provinces.
I am sure the Prime Minister will agree that the constitutional field is within the provinces, and the dominion's only excuse for stepping in, I assume, is the fear that the provinces will not undertake or carry out the job in a satisfactory manner, perhaps for lack of funds. The dominion now has almost a monopoly of the whole taxation power, under arrangements made since this war started; the taxation field of the provinces has become extremely limited and narrowed. The dominion now is in a position to finance works for reconstruction and rehabilitation, but in provincial circles there is a strong feeling that the autonomy of the provinces ought to be respected. Nowhere, I think, is that feeling more prominent than in the old province of Quebec, where they have always been very jealous of their autonomy, and rightly so. There has been a constant encroachment upon their rights.
I do say to the Prime Minister that there is a good deal of padding and filling in section 9, that he has all the powers he needs without that. If he would limit it to subsection (c) I would not have a word to say; for I think it should be limited to matters of administration.

speechtext:
Section 9 reads:
The governor in council may make such order or regulation as may be deemed necessary or advisable-
Last week we considered a bill to establish a department of veterans' affairs, of which section 7 read as follows:
Subject to the approval of the governor in council, the minister may make such regulations, from time to time, as he may deem necessary and advisable-
In this section the words are "such order or regulation" while in the other bill the words were, "such regulations." All regulations made hereunder approved by the governor in council shall be laid before parliament within fifteen days after they are made if parliament is then sitting, and if not, then within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing .session thereof.

I wish the Prime Minister would give some consideration to that point. subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although I am a member of the reconstruction committee I have not made a speech of any length on this subject of reconstruction. I am in agreement with the setting up of this department. Section 9(b) provides for the setting up of boards or advisory councils to exercise such Junctions in connection with the administration of this act as may be assigned to them by order or regulation. It is in connection with this section that I should like to make one suggestion to the Prime Minister with which I believe he will be in general agreement.
We have had a great deal of discussion during the past while about the problem of giving employment to our people. I agree that a need exists in connection with the basic foundation of our whole life-that is, employment for our men and women so that they will have adequate wages and a chance to live decently. But I think in this connection the Prime Minister will also agree that we cannot neglect the other side. There is the well known quotation that man cannot live by bread alone. One thing which the Atlantic charter has promised to mankind generally is that in the new era which opens-before us man shall not only live; he shall have life more abundantly.
We cannot leave the whole question of reconstruction without recognizing the cultural side of Canadian life. Just last week the committee on reconstruction had before it representatives of cultural groups in Canada who presented one of the most comprehensive-briefs yet placed before that committee. They outlined the possibilities which lie before the people of Canada in this direction. Their brief contained two main premises. The first was that in our relationship with the rest of' the world Canada needs to become cognizant of the fact that her cultural activities will be of assistance in maintaining friendly relations-

Department of Reconstruction
with other nations. Second, the cultural development of our people will help to give them that more abundant life which we believe can and must be theirs.
This group of artists, musicians and other representatives of cultural groups asked that a sum of money be set aside for these purposes. They were asking for only a small amount, merely $10,000,000, with which they hoped to start a planned system of what might be called adult education under which the natural talent and abilities of the Canadian people might be directed and encouraged by government supervision. They advised the setting up of community centres where there would be cultural and recreational activities, particularly in the rural areas where we have had such a dearth of culture.
There is in this proposal I believe the realization of how much can be done in the future toward binding together the peoples who make up Canada. There is the great cultural heritage of the province of Quebec, which is perhaps more typically Canadian than any other section of the country. Those people should be welded with the Anglo-Saxon, with the Ukrainian, with the Scandinavian, with the Polish, and with members of other minority groups. Not only would this give the Canadian people a new vision and a new outlook upon life itself; it would be a means of providing employment to many hundreds of people who possibly have no way by which they can give to this country of their natural talent and ability except through the channels of music or art or literature. Definitely I am of the opinion that a start should be made now, perhaps with the creation of a separate branch to deal with cultural relations and cultural matters. I believe that a beginning can be made at this time by the setting up under this section of a national arts board, so that the Minister of Reconstruction, whoever he may be, might have members of cultural groups in this country to advise him and give assistance in the various things which might be accomplished during an era of reconstruction.
Certainly when you think of the question of international trade you begin to realize that in competition with some of the other countries-the United States, for example, and Britain perhaps-we might suffer in this country from having other people take our designs and use them, and being themselves in a position to produce more cheaply than we could, thereby stealing our trade. Industry in Canada should be protected; and I feel that in the field of design there is a need for laws to protect Canadian artists and whatever
they may be able to accomplish by way of industrial development. It would be very necessary I think to have a board to take care of matters of this kind.
I mentioned the other day in the committee, when this group was before us, that there may be some things attributable to the Chinese for which they are not responsible. But at all events I believe the Chinese have a saying which goes something like this: that if a poor man has two yen, it is wiser for his soul's sake that he spend only one yen to buy a loaf of bread and that with the other he buy a rose. I believe that in the hurried rush of the years the people of Canada have been intent upon the bread and have as yet paid little attention to the rose. Although some hon. members may think this unrealistic,
I would definitely place before the Prime Minister the importance of realizing the vast possibilities of the Canadian people whose talents and abilities could be given expression to through cultural channels, and I should like to see set up under section 9 of this bill a national arts board, so that this aspect of reconstruction shall not be overlooked.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
There is just one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister; it is one which has been before the house on previous occasions and has to do with the question of the delegation of legislative powers to a minister of the crown.
The Prime Minister to-day pointed out that the reason for his change of opinion was that with time there had been a change of circumstances that made it necessary to confer on ministers of the crown legislative authority to make law, and in certain cases to make substantive law. I would point out to him that similar conditions exist in the United Kingdom. Actually the legislative field in the United Kingdom is much wider than that which this parliament has, and although the United Kingdom is legislating for a very much larger population than Canada's; it has not yet gone on an order in council spree to the extent that Canada has. The total number of orders in council and regulations made in the United Kingdom since the war began is not more than some 6,700, if my information is correct, while in Canada the number is approximately 43,000.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert has made out a good case for the addition to this bill of a provision which, while recognizing the necessity for a degree of delegation, nevertheless will retain in parliament control over the legislative powers delegated to the minister. A commendable step was taken by the Prime
Department o) Reconstruction

Minister some months ago when a suggestion of mine was accepted that an appendix or list be made up at the end of each session setting out the orders in council which had been passed. This has been of great assistance, not only to members of the judiciary and the legal profession, but to the citizens in general; because so many orders in council have been passed during the war interfering with the exercise of substantive rights that few lawyers were until recently in a position to advise with authority on the state of the law at any given time. The publication of this list or appendix has at least made available the sources of the new legislation, and as such has been helpful.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert suggested that there should be a provision, similar to that contained in a bill previously introduced, under which a report is to be made to parliament of the orders in council as passed. While he was speaking I sent out for the report of the committee on ministers' powers, presented by the Lord High Chancellor to the British parliament in April, 1932. That report supports the request of the hon. member for St. John-Albert and reinforces him in the stand that he has taken. On page 67 of this report, following the admission that the complexities of modern legislative authority make it necessary that there be a degree of delegation, particularly in matters of technical or special legislation, this distinguished royal commission says:
There should be uniform procedure in regard to all regulations required to be laid before parliament, namely, that they should be open to annulment-not modification-by resolution of either house within twenty-eight days on which the house has sat, such annulment to [DOT]be without prejudice to the validity of any action already taken under the regulation which is annulled.
Then it goes on to make this further recommendation. Recognizing the necessity for delegation of powers in order to cover eventualities that could not be contemplated by parliament, it says:
Standing orders of both houses should require that a small standing committee should be set up in each house of parliament at the beginning of each -session for -the purpose of-
(A)	considering and reporting on every bill containing a proposal to confer law-making power on a minister:
(B)	considering and reporting on every regulation and rule made in the exercise of delegated legislative power, and laid before the house in pursuance of statutory requirement.
It further points out that a standing committee looking into these regulations would only report on the question whether any matter of principle was involved, whether there was any special feature of the regulation

or rule meriting the attention of the house, and whether the regulation or rule should receive special consideration on the ground that it was exceptional in its legislative power and result. I realize that in war time we have gone a long way in delegating authority. We have not only delegated authority to ministers but have delegated wide authority to boards not directly responsible to parliament-indeed to such a dangerous extent that the actions of these boards, however illegal they -may be, are not subject to examination by the courts. I am sure the Prime Minister will not contest what I say, because throughout the years, as I read Hansard of previous parliaments, he was the great protagonist of the retention by parliament, in parliament, of legislative authority.
Now that we can believe that peace will not be too long removed, we in parliament must again examine strictly all delegations of authority which are proposed to be effective in peace time. I submit that while, recognizing the necessity of delegation to cover unusual circumstances or conditions which are bound to arise and cannot be foreseen, on all sides of the house there will be agreement that the exercise of delegated authority should be circumscribed in order to ensure that interference with private rights shall not take place without an opportunity being given to parliament to examine the regulations pertaining thereto, to the end that parliament may retain to the largest possible extent the legislative function.
This is not a controversial matter. If in all our statutes containing a delegation of authority it be provided that so far as such delegated legislative authority is concerned the terms of the pertinent orders in council be laid on the table of parliament, it would go a long way toward removing the present objection that few of us have the opportunity of knowing what is being done under the delegated authority conferred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I agree with
very much of what my hon. friend has said. I thank him for having expressed the view that I was a great protagonist for retaining in parliament the necessary legislative authority in these matters. May I say to him that I shall become more strongly than ever a protagonist of retaining as much power as possible in parliament once we get to a time that it is possible for parliament to cope with the many matters which come before it. Parliament at a time of war, could not cope with all the matters which require decision, and to a lesser degree, but still a very considerable

Department oj Reconstruction
degree, will require decision in a time of reconstruction. The power to delegate, in any event, has to be authorized in the first instance by parliament.
I do not yield a particle of the view that I have held on the supremacy of parliament and the need of preserving the control of parliament over the ministry, and of the ministry preserving to the full its responsibility. But I am surprised that the hon. member should attempt to estimate the extent of the legislation under order in council by the numbers of orders in council which are passed rather than by what is contained in them. If he does not mind my saying it, that seems to be an aibsurd method of estimating in any true way the quality or amount of legislation. To judge these things by the numbers of orders passed is, I think, proceeding in a quite erroneous way. One enactment might require no end of orders to meet a mass of detail, whereas another would take a much broader scope and not require anything like the same amount of detail to be dealt with by orders.
My hon. friend compares the extent of legislation by order in council in Britain and Canada, but the reason that so many more orders in council are passed here is that in Britain the minister of a department is given powers which in Canada can only be exercised by authority of the governor in council as a whole. We shall find as time goes on that it will be essential for this parliament more and more in that regard to follow the example of the United Kingdom parliament, and to trust ministers with responsibility, rather than to limit a minister's action and authority by requiring, in regard to many matters of detail, that these powers are to be exercised only by the governor in council as a whole. That is the real reason why orders in council are so much less numerous in Britain than they are here.
As to the publication of what is enacted by order in council or by delegated authority under regulation, I have already referred to a general order in council which, I think, covers the matter. May I read, however, from the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 162, the Public Printing and Stationery' Act, section 29, the following, which seems to me also to cover what the hon. members for Lake Centre and St. John-Albert have requested:
All proclamations issued by the governor general or under the authority of the governor in council, and all official notices, orders in council, regulations, advertisements and documents relating to the Dominion of Canada, or matters under the control of the parliament thereof, and requiring publication, shall be published in the Canada Gazette, unless some other mode of publication thereof is required by law.
So that there is already the provision made under a general statute for the publication of regulations.
A comparison has been made between the bill respecting the establishment of the Department of Veterans' Affairs and this bill establishing a Department of Reconstruction. There is this difference, which is a very important one. The legislation respecting the Department of Veterans' Affairs is of the nature of permanent legislation; the department is being established for a long time to come. The present legislation is in the nature of what is temporary legislation. The measure specifically states that this legislation shall not be in force for a period longer than is regarded as essential to tide over the period of reconstruction, and that period is estimated at about four years. That, I think, is a substantial reason why one would not expect to find, in a measure which relates to a situation which is temporary, some of the provisions which do exist in regard to a measure such as the Veterans' Affairs Act.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I want to ask four questions. First, what will be the powers of the new minister in connection with works which might be considered international? For instance, if it is decided by the two countries to provide work, and the proposed conservation work is that-for which plans and specifications are fully prepared-for the raising of the levels of lake Erie by building a dam across the Niagara river, would this new ministry have any powers to negotiate in that connection? That is international. Second, in connection with interprovincial works such as-the rehabilitation of the Saskatchewan river- and it is something that must be done, something that has been too long neglected,, something that the whole country owes to the west, the placing of that river under control so as to enable it to perform what in my judgment is its God-given function, that of assisting the west-what will be the powers of the new minister in an interprovincial labour problem of that magnitude? Third, what will be his powers in a purely provincial-municipal programme such as the flood-proofing and. water conservation works of the Thames or any other river in Ontario or any other province? Finally, in connection with industry, the post-war planning information sent out by the war-time information board refers to the reconstruction period after the war, and among other statements it declares that the object is to encourage private enterprise. The report recommends that the corporation profita tax and the excess profits tax be eliminated at
Department of Reconstruction

the earliest possible moment. It recommends the removal as soon as possible of controls designed to restrict consumption.
All this is essential if industry is to have an opportunity to go forward and, as the Prime Minister so well said in his opening remarks, take a larger place in providing employment during the reconstruction period. If industry does that, it will conform to the principles laid down at the conference at which the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Prime Minister of Russia and the President of the United States declared for a stable peace with full employment and the raising of the standard of living. I would impress upon the Prime Minister the importance of these four matters which I have brought to his attention -international projects, interprovincial programmes, provincial-municipal works, and abolishing war-time regulations, as suggested in the post-war planning information sent out by the war-time information board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
The powers the minister will have in regard to all these matters are set out in sections 5 and 6 already passed. I do not wish to evade giving a full answer, but that would be an appropriate reply at this moment. The minister, broadly speaking, will do all that he thinks advisable and desirable in the way of coordinating efforts which will lead towards full employment and reconstruction, whether in the field of international affairs, interprovincial affairs, or intermunicipal affairs, so far as these might be in any way related to the work of reconstruction carried on by the federal administration. In other words, if the minister thought in connection with some international project that it would be possible to further employment to a greater extent in one particular way rather than another and that the way he had in mind would involve the consideration of authorities in another country, he would bring that matter to the attention of his colleagues in the cabinet and the international aspect would in the first instance, be dealt with, if the cabinet approved, by the Department of External Affairs, which has responsibility for international negotiations. Similarly, as between the provinces and the dominion, the minister would see that there were conferences arranged of a kind which he thought desirable to bring the province and the dominion together to discuss those matters that might further reconstruction. Similarly also with regard to the municipalities. This act does not give the minister arbitrary powers of a kind that no minister of the crown possesses to-day, but it does give him the

fullest authority to get in touch with as many other authorities as may be possible where he sees an opportunity of coordinating work which thereby will more efficiently further reconstruction.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: The Prime Minister referred just now to an order in council having been passed providing that orders in council shall be published. Surely the one he is referring to deals with orders and regulations passed under the War Measures Act. These have been published and they have been of the greatest use. I do not think that order in council covers such orders and regulations as are referred to in a bill of this sort, and it se'ems to be most essential that the public should be able to find out what regulations and orders are passed1 under a measure such as this. I consider it parallel to the other one we dealt with the other day arranging for veterans' affairs. There it is enacted in the measure that regulations shall be published, and it seems to me a most desirable thing that these orders and regulations should somehow see the light of day. It is so difficult for the public, apart from lawyers who may have ability and facilities which the ordinary man has not got, to ascertain what regulations have been passed. To the ordinary member of the public who desires to look up a certain subject it is most difficult to find out what has actually been passed in the way of regulations.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: A moment ago I read from the revised statutes the particular section of the act dealing with printing and publishing which necessitates the publication of orders and regulations, and the like, in the Canada Gazette.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS

There is a
comma, "or matters under the control of the parliament thereof, and requiring publication".

Department oj Reconstruction

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That means if publication is deemed to be required. That endorses the statement of the hon. member for Yale.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
That leaves a loophole, that it is in the discretion of certain people to publish or not to publish. Why is it put in one statute and not in another? Clearly, a strict construction of the section which the right hon. gentleman has just read indicates that these matters may not all be published, and certainly they are not all published.
I did not intend to speak again, but the Prime Minister renewed his faith in parliamentary institutions. On one celebrated occasion within recent months he slipped. I may forgive him that, because it is said that even Homer nods. But his government passed an order in peace time altering a civil statute that had nothing to do with the war at all. In March of last year an amendment to the Companies Act was put through which altered the law, and I doubt if it ever saw the light of day until somebody dug it up. Did that come to the attention of the Prime Minister, and did he give his imprimatur to it? It was done because the Minister of Transport desired to seize jurisdiction unknown to the people of Canada and to the legal profession. On examination the Prime Minister will find out that it is not all as he would suggest it is. Things are being done to-day by order in council which ought never to be done. I make that statement to the Prime Minister in general terms. I know he cannot watch everything that goes through council. He cannot be there every day. He has to take the statement of his minister on the recommendations and reports that are made by various departments; but there are official acts given the imprimatur of the governor in council as to matters unrelated to the war that ought never to be approved. That is what we object to. I realize that the government must have large and important powers to carry on the war, and emergent powers in relation to those other things that they have set up, although I do not concur in the theory. Powers are delegated to boards that are created, and those powers are not reviewable by the courts. That is an offence committed by the government in relation to certain boards that have been set up during this war. They are not even open to question by the courts. The subject is denied access to the courts. That is a pretty serious thing to happen in this country. On general principles the Prime Minister will agree with that. Denial of access to the courts of Canada should in no
circumstances be made, and no government which thinks the thing through would ever permit that sort of thing to be done.
I know in days gone by that governments have seized jurisdiction. I suppose no greater controversy ever arose in the United States than arose when Mr. Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus at one stage in the civil war. No action on the part of his government, in theory at least, ever raised such a controversy as the seizure of power by his administration at that time. I say to the government, let us forget about the past in regard to these things and let us not have a repetition of what has been done improperly in days gone by, especially on the question referred this afternoon to by the hon. member for Lake Centre, the denial to the citizens of this country of access to the courts. I agree with the underlying principle of this section that there should be secrecy in relation to the business of any person, and that information of a private nature or relating to a private business, an individual business or a corporation, should not be disclosed, for Teasons which I think will commend themselves to everyone. But I gravely question the provisions of section 11. I wish the Prime .Minister would direct his attention to that.

What is meant by the words "without lawful excuse"? Suppose the minister demands certain information which I do not wish to give. Notwithstanding the provisions with respect to secrecy, in section 10, we know that it is impossible to keep all this information secret, and I protest against the provision that a man who refuses to speak shall be found guilty of an offence against the act. On general principles that provision is bad.
I will give the Prime Minister an illustration of what I mean. Recently the wartime prices and trade board sent out to shook manufacturers a questionnaire including dozens upon dozens of questions, calling upon them, under the authority of some order in council, to disclose to that board the fullest possible information about these individual businesses. This is information which is given to-day only to the taxation department, and which ought not to be given even to the department in the detail required in this instance save and except on the theory that it is necessary to protect the public revenue. Here the wartime prices and trade board are asking me, as a box manufacturer, to disclose my business in great detail to an army of officials-because that is what it will come down to in its final essence; and while I know an attempt is made in the regulations to hide the identity of the individual by using a code number, or something of the kind, still I say it is asking just too much of human nature. I can tell the Prime Minister that in the case I mentioned the demand will be thoroughly ineffective, because in eastern Canada at least the shook business is not distinct and apart; it is wrapped up with, it is a corollary or branch of, the lumber business. As a rule shooks are made from the lumber left over from the general trade, and they are set up in one corporate enterprise. It is impossible to break that down, from an accounting standpoint; therefore what is required is the disclosure to the wartime prices and trade board of information they ought not to have, because it is information relating to a much broader subject matter and information which, if it came to the notice of a competitor, might do a great deal of damage to the subject under review.
Without pursuing the subject further I ask the Prime Minister to state upon what principle he suggests that this house should enact a punitive clause against some of the people of this country for refusing to give information with respect to a broad subject such as reconstruction. Of course any good citizen will comply with a proper request, but it might go far beyond that; it might become an inquisition in the hands of an improper official. I do think this is going a long, long way, and

that the Prime Minister would never tolerate it in his own private business. Certainly I would be quite against it, if I came up against a statutory provision of this sort, that because I found it in my own interests and in the interests of my shareholders, we will say, that I should not answer certain questions put to me by the minister, I should be classed as a quasi-criminal and made subject to a penalty. If you can imagine any more bureaucratic method of carrying on business than legislation of this type, I should like to know what it is. I suggest to the Prime Minister that if the public knew this provision was in the bill they would condemn this legislation out of hand, not because on its face it is not a good measure but because attention would be diverted from the good features of the bill to this drastic feature which I suggest should be eliminated.
What reasonable excuse is there for putting in this provision? It ought not to be there at all. The minister has all kinds of power to get advice, to set up committees and do everything else that may be necessary. I cannot imagine why this provision should be included, why it should foe fastened upon a long-suffering public in the face of all the regimentation, the regulation and the bureaucracy we have in this country to-day. That is the sort of thing that is killing government; that is the sort of thing the Prime Minister is going to meet when he goes to the country. I am not particularly anxious to help the Prime Minister when he goes to the country, but if I had no other canvass against this government I would not want a better one than this question of regimentation and bureaucracy.
A moment ago I was facetious; now I am serious, and I do suggest to the Prime Minister that he consider the elimination of section 11. It is undemocratic; it is unnecessary; it is uncalled for. I cannot think of a single useful purpose it will serve. As to the secrecy of information, of course I commend section 10, but certainly I intend to vote against section 11.

I suggest to the Prime Minister that it is a fundamental principle of British justice that when a charge is laid against a man for an infracton of the criminal code, of a quasi criminal piece of legislation or for the commission of a prohibited act, the burden is on the crown, not on the subject. This is on a par with the old prohibitory laws we borrowed from Texas, and other places like Texas, where they had the sumptuary type of legislation which takes away from the subject all his rights and puts him upon the defensive the minute an information is laid. This is not the type of legislation we ought to have if we expect cooperation from the people of Canada.

Yes; quite true. I want to
tell the Minister of Justice, because I take him to be a man of the cities rather than of the country, that when he deals with the cities he generally finds that the justices of the peace or local magistrates are men of some considerable knowledge of law, either lawyers or having some practical experience in law offices or the like of that; but in the country the situation is quite different. In the country men are often appointed simply to meet the need of having someone available to acknowledge a deed, or a conveyance in the case of a man selling a piece of property, when he has to acknowledge his signature before a justice of the peace. Those are about the principal purposes for which they are appointed. Occasionally they deal with the odd drunk, but that is a very simple matter. The justice of the peace, I submit, in all kindness to them- many of them are my personal friends-do not know the law. When there is so much uncertainty among experts as we have seen this afternoon, how do you expect a country storekeeper or game warden or someone of that kind to be familiar with the law? These men may be well educated, but that does not teach them the law. I will give you three instances, two of which came within my personal knowledge and the other was well advertised.
I am myself a magistrate, although I have not acted for many years. On one occasion I had to get a justice of the peace to sit with me on a case, since it required the presence of two justices of the peace, and I had a horrible time persuading my brother magistrate not to send the three defendants, who were charged with something not very much worse than a bad drunk, to penal servitude for fourteen years. He was a capable, sensible

man, but he did not know anything about the law. We finally compromised on three months.
On another occasion, in a little country place some petty ill-feeling led a man to lay a charge against another man for the theft of a mink trap. The trap was worth only fifteen cents new, and this was a second-hand one. The case got before a justice of the peace; a small settlement took sides, and in the end the whole thing was remitted to a court about one hundred and fifty miles away. The justice of the peace was told to serve subpoenas upon the crown witnesses, and in his broad, generous mind he thought he would act fairly and issued summonses to everybody, including witnesses for the defence. By this time the entire village had divided itself into two clans, and nearly half the residents went down to the trial and had a nice holiday. In the end it cost the provincial government $500 to decide the ownership of that mink trap. I have forgotten what happened to the trap, but I know it cost the provincial government $500 because the case came before a country justice of the peace who had the best of intentions.
I give another instance, and it comes home to the hon. member for Yale because it occurred in his district. There are several large lakes there, and a man was charged with the theft of a boat or canoe worth not more than $10. The case was brought before the local justice of the peace, a thoroughly educated gentleman also animated with the best of intentions. The accused was his personal friend; they had social relations with each other. The magistrate thumbed over the criminal code and said to the accused, "I am awfully sorry, old man, but the nearest case I can find to yours is piracy on the high seas and that is punishable with death. I don't know what else can be done." If somebody had not interfered, I suppose the man would have been sentenced to the extreme penalty. These are facts, and this is only an illustration.
Now, you cannot expect knowledge of the law on the part of a country justice of the peace, and yet you are going to give him the power to punish a man with a fine of $500 or in the case of a firm $5,000-and it is sometimes popular but not always wise to hit the big firm in a country place. I suggest that the offence ought to be made indictable. If the Minister of Justice will think the matter over I believe he will agree with me. This is tricky legislation; it is a new measure for which there is no precedent; the justice of the peace cannot run his finger down the page of any statute and find comparable offences. It is entirely new. These cases are not likely

Department oj Reconstruction
to any great extent to come before country justices of the peace, and in the towns a higher authority will be easily accessible. It would be very much better to have the prosecution made under indictment and not under summary conviction, because this would bring it before a judge who has knowledge of the law.
It might be said that it is necessary to impose heavy penalties in order to enforce the law, but it does not by any means follow that by putting absurdly heavy penalties within the discretion of an untrained man you are going to have a successful enforcement of a statute. The minister at the present time has before the house a bill for the amendment of an act which has been on the statutes for fifty or sixty years, which provide that if a man is caught stealing anything, however small, from a letter in the mails, he shall go to the penitentiary for not less than three years, and he explained when he introduced the bill that it had been found necessary to amend the law because as it stood it was not fair to the petty thief and did not result in a successful enforcement of the provision. The reason for that is obvious. Rather than send a man to gaol for three years for a trivial offence a magistrate will suspend sentence, or the matter will be hushed up. That is what I am impressing on the minister now. If he makes his.punish-ment too heavy the penalty will not be enforced, because the matter is likely to be hushed up. It is said of a certain ruler of Turkey that, having found a baker giving false weight, he had the man put into his own oven and baked, and he said that he had stopped that crime for the future. Well, that is neither the British nor the Christian way of doing things. In the long run, certainty of punishment, rather than undue severity, is what deters crime, and I suggest to the minister that what we should aim at here is certainty rather than unduly harsh punishment. For that reason I suggest that the matter should be taken by way of indictment.

LAURENT: An indictable offence is usually looked upon as much, more serious than matters that are punishable by summary conviction, and this here was regarded merely as an offence and not as something which formerly would have been considered a felony. It having been declared an offence, a penalty had to be provided in the bill itself, or the penalty would have been that fixed by the criminal code under section 164, which is much severer than the one here set out.

I should like to make a few remarks on the general question that is dealt with in this section. May I read it so that it will appear on Hansard.
The expenses of administration of this act and any other expenditures to be made by the department or by any other department hereunder shall be met out of the war appropriation or other moneys appropriated by parliament.
The other night I took occasion to comment upon the wording of paragraph (e) of section 2, which reads:
"reconstruction" means the reestablishment in civil life and reemployment on demobilization of the men and women of the armed services, of persons released from war industries, and the reorganization of industry, in ordeT to provide maximum production and full employment during and following the change over from war-time production of industry to peace-time production, and includes every undertaking by dominion, provincial or municipal authority or by any corporation or other person which may contribute to such reorganization.
May I call the committee's attention to the very wide field which is covered by paragraph (e) of section 2, and the enormous expenditure of money which will be involved? I doubt very much whether the average member of this committee, including myself, can form even a vague guess of the astronomical figure

which will be required to express the amount of money which would bring about full employment in Canada. Notice what it says: . . . maximum production and full employment during and following the change over from war-time production . . .
I am raising the question, where is the money coming from? If I may direct my remarks for a few minutes constructively to the proposal that the money must not come entirely from debt or taxation, I may make a worth-while contribution to the proceedings of this committee.
I believe it is well known by the members of this committee that tihe organization which I represent in this house believes in the use of the national credit for the financing of projects which are incidental to raising the standard of living in the country; that it maintains that money can be created by the state debt-free-or shall we say "currency" instead of money; and that the amount of such money that can be created bears a direct relation to the productive and consumptive capacity of the nation. If it is accepted that the amount of currency or money which a nation can create depends directly upon the goods and services which that nation can produce and consume, then we reach a realistic concept of the amount of money which the government may have available for the prosecution of any project which it may deem advisable.
We have a way of determining the amount of money we can have, because the amount will depend upon our resources and our skill in working up those resources into consumable goods which our people and people abroad can enjoy. May I cite to the Prime Minister two or three little excerpts from documents which I believe he will find thoroughly reliable and authentic? First I suggest that he take the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada of 1933 and turn to page 22, paragraph 47. There he will read the following words:
In the war session of August, 1914, parliament raised the partially covered issue to $50,000,000. Subsequently an issue of $16,000,000 was made against the deposit of railway securities guaranteed by the dominion government, as well as an uncovered issue of $10,000,000 for government purposes.
May I pause just there to reason with the Prime Minister for a minute or two on what is contained in that statement? The only backing behind the 316,000,000 was railway securities; and behind the $10,000,000 there was no backing at all. But the $26,000,000 which were produced as a result of this creation of money were spent by the government

Department of Reconstruction
for governmental purposes. That was back during the last war, in a time when ordinarily it is dangerous for the state to create money, because there is usually or likely to be a scarcity of goods in the country while war is progressing. May I continue with the passage:
In 1917 an emergency issue of $50,000,000 of dominion notes was made to finance war purchases in Canada by the British government. The notes were secured by imperial treasury bills. In due course, this indebtedness was liquidated by payments from the British treasury and all of this issue had been redeemed by 1927.
That passage has no particular bearing on the matter under discussion this afternoon. The next passage is:
No changes have since been made in the Dominion Notes Act except that by a statute passed on March 30, 1933, the governor in council was empowered to suspend the redemption in gold of dominion notes, and an order in council to this effect was made on April 10, 1933.
It is to be gathered from that passage that after April 10, 1933, it was no longer possible for any one holding a Dominion of Canada note to demand gold in redemption of it. This put the country on a fiat money basis purely and simply, and roughly speaking the country has so continued from that time to the present.
What is there behind the fiat money which can give it stability and value? Only the goods and services producing power of the nation; for the more goods and services a nation can produce the more readily is it possible to buy goods with the money which the nation may create. This truth has profound significance for Canada in the post-war period. It will have a tremendous importance in its bearing upon this act if it is applied successfully, and I wish the Prime Minister and anyone who is in power in the country during the post-war period every success in the application of it. But a tremendously important part in the successful application of this act and the achievement of the objective which is envisaged by it will be played by created money, debt-free. I warn the Prime Minister or anyone who holds his position during those trying times that if we in Canada must depend upon the money which can be collected by taxation from the Dominion of Canada for the application of this act, then the whole process of reconstruction will be a disappointment of the bitterest kind, and many of the fine ideals which actuated those who framed this bill will be discarded, because men will rise and say: "The war is over; we have to pay for the war. Let us tighten our belts." Immediately there will be induced a period of retrenchment
100-262i
which will bode ill for the success of the application of this act and will tend to results as deplorable as those which resulted from the last war.
On one or two occasions I have offended the Prime Minister by rather severe remarks directed towards the way in which we were treating the returned men of the last war. I do not propose to refer to them this afternoon. I have not changed my opinion one iota. The men who fought the last war were my friends, my companions, the boys who were my age, my school mates, my university companions; and the way those men were treated after the war will be held by me as a condemnation of the administrations which have conducted affairs in Canada since that time. Offhand I cannot recall a single man who-received the treatment to which he was entitled. The Prime Minister knows we promised these men "homes for heroes." He has read of that, but what returned man ever received a home befitting a hero?
Now may I go on with this general question of the creation of money, just to show what there is in the records which are available to all hon. members of this house. I wish to-quote further from the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, this time at pages 22 and 23, and to read what was said by a former minister of finance of the dominion government, a man for whom I should think the Liberals in particular would have a high degree of respect:
But extensive use continued to be made of the power to issue dominion notes to the -banks against approved securities with the result that it was decided in 1923 to make this part of the Finance Act mechanism a feature of the normal Canadian financial system. In introducing the new legislation, Mr. Fielding, -the Minister of Finance, made the following -brief explanation of its purpose: "The act (Finance Act) was-adopted as a war measure, and no doubt was-exceedingly useful in the financial operations-during the war. It may be said that the war being over we no longer have any need for the act, but experience has shown that the act is still required; indeed, I am inclined to think that something of -the kind will have to become almost a permanent -part of our financial system."
I wonder why the Liberal party has so long neglected the wise counsel implied in those words. May I now refer to another semiofficial document, the Canada Year Book, 1932, at the bottom of 759, where hon. members will find a footnote containing the following, words:
The Finance Act, 1914 (5 Geo. Y.C. 3) makes-provision in case of war, panic, etc., -for the issue of dominion notes against approved securities. This emergency arrangement was made a permanent feature by c. 48 of -the statutes of 1923.

Department oj Reconstruction

One cannot help but wonder why, before we allowed our returned men to suffer degradation, we did not use these powers. I believe the fact that we did not do so constitutes a solemn warning to this generation that unless something is done we will continue to ignore these possibilities. I must say that I am really discouraged by reason of the fact that the Prime Minister, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Cariboo, who were the government representatives and advocates in the discussion which preceded the introduction of this bill and in the discussion of the bill itself, referred to nothing but taxation and debt. In a vague sort of way the hon. member for Cariboo reminded us what the banks did when they had to market a crop of wheat, but beyond that he did not go, nor did the Prime Minister. What does it mean? It means that the people of Canada are left out on a limb at the present time, with no idea whatever of how the government proposes to do all the things it envisages in this act. If the government has no financial device for financing the projects involved in this act, beyond borrowing and taxation, all I can say is that this whole measure is nothing in the world but another means of deceiving the Canadian people.
As an indication of the possibilities of the use of debt-free money, state-created, I should like to read two or three passages from the report of the Bank of Canada dated February 10, 1944, wherein the governor of the bank, or whoever wrote the report, suggests the tremendous productive capacity of Canada in the post-war world. I have already indicated that the amount of money a state can create debt-free depends upon the goods the state can produce and consume. If, then, it can be shown that we are capable of producing an astounding amount of goods, them the possibility of the use of this debh-free money, which is indicated in the three excerpts which I have read, becomes very encouraging. Now I read from page 11 of the report of the Bank of Canadla:
By the end of 1943 the gainfully occupied population had risen to approximately 5,100,000 but about 1,900,000 of these were engaged in tile armed forces, in supplying the weapons of war, or in producing the food required for special wartime exports. The number available to meet civilian needs 'had therefore fallen to about 3,200,000, but at the same time the average standard of living had risen materially and was *probably higher than it had ever been.
