This discrepancy may be accounted for by two factors: (a) the level of employment and incomes was slightly lower during the year than was anticipated at the time of making the budget forecast; and (b) the amount of taxes refunded during the year as a result of the cancellation of 50 per cent of the 1942 liability under the transition to the "pay-as-you-go" system was larger than had been anticipated. These refunds are deducted from the revenue of the year in which they are repaid, and the amount shown for 1943-44 has thus been reduced by the amount of such repayments.
At the present time it is estimated that the savings portion of personal income taxes levied against 1943 incomes and repayable to the taxpayer after the end of the war was in the neighbourhood of $110,000,000. It was estimated in the previous year that the corresponding amount in relation to 1942 incomes

would be $50,000,000, which it is now proposed, on the basis of more complete information, to increase by an additional amount of $5,000,000. These amounts taken together thus give an estimate' of the total amount refundable on the dominion's books at the end of the fiscal year 1943-44 of $165,000,000 repayable after the war in respect of the 1942 and 1943 taxation years.
9.	Corporate income tax and excess profits tax, both of which are levied on business incomes, may appropriately be discussed together. Revenue from the corporate income tax amounted to $311,379,000, slightly in excess of the forecast of $300,000,000, but below revenue of the previous year by $36,591,000. This decline was due to the fact that in the previous year collections were somewhat above normal because of inauguration of the compulsory monthly plan of tax payment in July, 1942, which brought forward into the fiscal year 1942-43 revenue which under the old system of one single annual payment would not have been received until the following fiscal year. In 1943-44, as the monthly payment plan was in effect for the full twelve months, there was no comparable overlapping of revenue, and collections were reduced to a level closer to normal.
Revenue from the excess profits tax, at $468,-
718,000	fell substantially below the forecast of $550,000,000 for the year. This discrepancy is largely explained by the extreme difficulty of forecasting from the distance of a ' year in advance not only the total amount of corporation profits during a year but also the extent t-o which such profits are excess profits, that is, in excess of standard profits. In th present instance it can only be said that because of these difficulties, for which there does not appear to be any ready solution, a substantial error was made in forecasting excess profits tax revenue for the fiscal year 1943-44.
It is now estimated that in respect of excess profits taxes collected in the fiscal year 194344 an amount of $40,000,000 will be refunded after the war. This figure can only be regarded as tentative until assessment of excess profits tax returns has been completed for the year in question, and the refundable amount finally determined in each case. It will be some time however before this work will be completed, and it is felt desirable in

The Budget-Appendix
the interim to establish on an estimated basis an approximate figure for the amount of such refundable taxes. The addition of this $40,000,000 to the $20,000,000 set up in the previous fiscal year brings to $60,000,000 the total amount of refundable taxes as at March 31, 1944.
10.	Revenue under the heading of dividends, interest, etc., is derived from the special taxes imposed on certain income under Section 9b of the Income War Tax Act. In 1943-44, this revenue amounted to $26,943,000, reduced by $1,138,000 from the previous year, and was derived for the most part from the 15 per cent tax levied on dividends and interest paid to non-residents.
11.	The dominion government has levied succession duties only since 1941, and revenue from this source is only gradually reaching its full anticipated level. Such revenue amounted to $15,020,000 in 1943-44, compared with $13,-
273,000	in the previous year.
12.	Small amounts of tax revenue are derived from the tax on note circulation of the chartered banks, which decreases from year to year -with the decline in such circulation as provided by statute; from taxes on the net premium income of insurance companies, reduced considerably in 1943-44 from the previous year because in the previous year two years' revenue was collected in one following certain arrangements made under the Dominion-Provincial Tax Agreements; from a tax on the export of electrical energy from Canada; and from a tax on the export of furs from the Northwest Territories. Revenue from all these taxes amounted in 1943-44 to $7,692,000.
13.	Total non-tax revenues are estimated at $139,865,000, an increase of $23,786,000 over 1942-43. Receipts from the Post Office total $61,071,000, an increase of approximately $12,-
200,000	which was due to the one cent increase in letter rates effective April 1, 1943, as well as to a greater volume of post-office business during the year. The receipts from the Post Office will, it is expected, exceed cost of operations by about $12,587,000 without taking into account any credit for services rendered other departments free of charge and without adding to the cost of operations, rentals and other costs of premises occupied by the Post Office. Returns on investments are expected to realize $52,152,000, an increase over the previous year of about $10,910,000. The larger items making up this total are: interest on advances to Canadian National Railways, $18,724,000; Bank of Canada profits, $14,118,000; interest on loans to Foreign Exchange Control Board, $3,467,000; interest
on loans to National Harbours Board, $3,250,000; interest on loans to provinces, $2,861,000; interest on loans to Canadian Farm Loan Board, $1,092,000; Soldier Land Settlement loans, $992,000; and interest on advances made by the Department of Munitions and Supply to commodity companies, $3,970,000.

14.	The total amount shown for the, fiscal year 1943-44 under this heading is $124,024,000. The items making up this total are: Special receipts, War Appropriation Acts, $81,000,000 (divided as follows: refunds of previous years' war expenditure, $32,500,000; sale of surplus war assets, $6,000,000; profits on certain war operations and miscellaneous war revenues, $42,500,000); operating surplus of the Canadian National Railways for the calendar year 1943, $35,640,000 and the capital gain on repatriation of Canadian National Railways securities, $2,430,000. These last two items increase the book valuation of the Canadian National Railways securities trust capital stock, and accordingly are offset by contra amounts appearing on the expenditure side under the heading "Other Charges".
The Canadian Pacific Railway company repaid a loan of $1,000,000 advanced under the authority of the Relief Act, 1932. This loan which was non-interest bearing was charged to non-active account and accordingly the repayment is shown as a revenue item.
Another item which is recorded under the heading of special receipts and credits is an amount of $2,971,000 representing a reduction in the reserve account established to meet the operating deficits of the Canadian Wheat Board. This adjustment is occasioned by a further improvement in the board's balance sheet based on calculations made as at July 31, 1943 with respect to the 1939 and 1940 crop accounts. This reserve account now stands at $8,816,210.36.

069,000	above referred to from the net operating revenue of $116,140,000, there remained a balance of $97,071,000. These two write-offs, and the provision for the further reserve of $25,000,000 resulted in a proportionate increase in the net debt of the dominion.
The total write-off from non-active assets includes two items: (a) $232,000 written off from the Canadian National Railways Securities Trust Stock representing line abandonments for the calendar year 1943; and (b) $29,000 representing the estimated yearly established losses on Seed Grain and Relief accounts administered by the Department of Mines and Resources. The Canadian National Railways Securities Trust Stock is carried in the dominion's books as a non-active asset, and as the two items just mentioned necessarily appear as credits under the heading Special Receipts and Credits, the net debt of Canada is not thereby changed.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words before this bill gets its third reading. There is no doubt that this new department which is to be set up is one of the most important acts that the government has performed so far this year. It has the prospect of being a very important department in the coming days after the war is over. This afternoon some hon. members expressed the opinion that this was not the time to be wasting our efforts in trying to set up anything in regard to reconstruction. It was suggested that that should not be done until the war had been definitely won. I do not agree with that idea. Along with the other hon. members of this party I say and have always maintained that the very first consideration of this country should be the successful prosecution of the war and that everything that is humanly possible should be done to facilitate that objective in every shape and form. While that is going on I would not agree with the opinion of the hon. member for Yrork-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) that at this time we should not make some preparations for the period after the war and that we should not be setting up a department of reconstruction. I think that is one of the necessary steps.
When the men and women of the armed forces come back they must be properly cared for. If we are to rehabilitate them as they have every right to expect, we must begin to prepare now. It will not do to wait until they return home and then start preparing.
I take it that in setting up the department at this time the government intends to start now. Unless we take some constructive and active action with regard to those who returned from the last war I fear we shall not do as much as we should do for those who come back from this war. I was very much impressed with the views expressed by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) this afternoon when he spoke of the veterans of the last war and advocated that they be given free titles to their land. He pointed out, and I think rightly so, that one of the first things that should be done is properly to care for those who came back from the last war, and then we could go on and prepare for those coming back from this war.
He pointed out that one of the government officials, with approval of the present Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), had made a statement to the effect that nothing could be done for those old veterans who are now on the land; that they should be satisfied and abide by the contracts into which they entered. That is not good enough for our returned men of the last war. If we are to use that as a precedent and treat the men and women coming back from this war in the same way, then I am afraid that things will not be arranged satisfactorily. I think we can rightly judge what the government is going to do in regard to the men and women returning from this war by what they have done for those who came back from the last war. I am sorry that such a statement should have been made by a government official at this time, because it certainly does not give those old veterans of the last war much encouragement.
It is true, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) has indicated in his budget speech this evening, that when a nation is at war it reaches the peak of production. We in this country are exceptionally fortunate in that we have never been invaded. We have not had those terrible air raids to contend with, nor have there been battlefields on our territory as is the case across the seas. Our productive capacity is at its maximum and will continue to be or should continue to be at its maximum until the war ends, because we have had nothing happen to this country which would affect that production. It is also true that when the war ends and the armed
Department of Reconstruction

forces are being demobilized the production of those industries will begin to slow down. As soon as those industries begin to slow down, and in some cases shut down entirely, a loss of purchasing power in the hands of the people immediately becomes evident, because the industries are beginning to release men from employment. These men become unemployed unless arrangements have been made to employ them in some other places. When the men and women of the armed forces return they, too, will be out of a job and their purchasing power will decrease. There you have a piling up of the unemployed; you have an ever-decreasing amount of purchasing power in the hands of the people, and the vicious circle begins which will lead us straight to the depression which we had before unless we make proper arrangements now. That is why I say I do not agree with some of the statements that have been made in this house to the effect that we should not prepare now; that all our attention should be given to the war.
Certainly no one in this house or outside it can point a finger at the Social Credit party and say that we have ever belittled our war effort in any sense of the word. In fact, we were the ones who were first for an all-out war effort and we are still for it. But at the same time I think we can and should begin to prepare now for the post-war period. Unless we are extremely careful we are bound to have after this wrar periods of depression with all the misery and poverty that go with them That is bound to happen unless we begin to prepare now. Therefore I say that one of the first things which must be done by this new department is to make a complete survej' forthwith to ascertain the nature and the volume of the products of industry which will be required by the Canadian people for purposes of rehabilitation after the war and to raise their standard of living to the level which our natural resources consistently can maintain. That is one of the first steps necessary; we must ascertain the nature and the volume. That entails a tremendous amount of research work. In my opinion there is no use in going to those industries now and saying to them that they must carry on their production after this war and that they must give full employment when no proper guidance has been given to them beforehand. . We should find out, for example-and I think we are capable of doing it with the intelligence we have here-the amount of farm machinery that it will be necessary to manufacture in Canada. We should be able to find out the number of automobiles that will be required in this 
country. When that is done we shall be able to go to those concerns and point out to them with some definiteness what will be required. Having that information, they in turn will be able to arrange and plan their production accordingly.
Not only will it be necessary for us to find out the nature and the volume of the production which can and should be carried on for our home markets, but there is a field farther away that must be thoroughly investigated so that those industries will be properly guided in their establishments after the war. The field I refer to is the foreign market. I think there will be a great potential market there if the industries are properly guided in that respect. Some provision will have to be made by this department to enable business firms to go farther afield, into those countries which have been ravaged by war and which have been released from the slavery and drudgery imposed by the enemy, in order to estimate the kind and volume of production that will be required from Canadian industry for those markets. Then, when our industries have that information, they will be in a much better position to carry on the work that is expected of them.
The next step which I think must be taken is a complete survey of Canadian industries to determine the extent to which they can be adapted to peace-time requirements, and to make the necessary preparations for conversion at the end of the war. I believe this is one of the most important steps that will have to be taken, but as far as I know nothing is being done along that line. It may be the intention of the minister in charge of this new department to carry on that work, but unless that is done I see great dangers ahead of us. For instance, I fear that after the war some of our great industries will close up, because they will not know what will be required of them. An example that comes to mind is the automobile manufacturing industry. I do not believe these companies will be able to continue, at least for very long, their present rate of production. There must be some survey made to determine whether these industries are capable of being adapted to some other type of production. Their equipment may be such that they can convert to the manufacture of farm implements. These plants should be surveyed very carefully; instead of having these big factories tom down and the machinery thrown on the junk heap, we should make every effort to convert them to peace-time production. Some may not be adapted to the production of farm machinery; some may be more adapted to the manufacture of cream

Department of Reconstruction
separators, or household requirements, or boots and shoes, or something else. Certainly I see a great danger that these industries may be scrapped instead of being properly converted to peace-time production. The other day, as reported at page 3980 of Hansard, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) dealt with that point; at least I believe it was in his mind, although I do not believe it has been given proper attention. He said:
There is one aspect of reconstruction which might be termed economic reconstruction. That *has to do largely with the transforming of industry from making war supplies to making goods for human consumption and with restoring and increasing the capital equipment of the nation, together with the provision of employment for those who are being transferred from the one activity to the other.
I believe that can be done if we have proper supervision. Then he went on to say:
The great industrial plant created for war purposes must be transformed to meet peacetime demands in Canada or abroad.
That is one of the matters to which I think great consideration must be given; otherwise we are not going to have the proper results. I am very much concerned about this. What are we doing in that regard? In my opinion we are doing just the reverse. What have we done so far in the matter of the actual preparation for the conversion of industries from wartime to peace-time production? The only concrete step we have taken so far has been to set up Surplus Crown Assets Corporation. In my opinion that corporation has not been set up primarily for the purpose of converting industry from war-time to peace-time production. It is only necessary to look at the bill to see the purpose for which the corporation has been set up, or at least what a large part of its work is going to be. I refer to section 12:
Subject to general or specific instructions given by the minister, the corporation may, when so directed by the minister,
(a) sell, exchange, lease, lend or otherwise dispose of or deal with surplus crown assets either gratuitously or for a consideration and upon such terms and subject to 6uch conditions as the board may consider desirable.
Some other recommendations are set out, but one of the purposes of the Crown Assets Corporation is to dispose of all this material; to get rid of the factories that now belong to the government, to deal with the machinery which is now in the possession of the government. I am not for a moment advocating that the government should take over these factories and this machinery and go into the production of consumer goods, but the whole purpose of the Crown Assets Corporation is to dispose of these assets without giving consideration to their conversion to peace-time production. I think that is bad; I do not believe these assets should be disposed of by the government in too much of a hurry. I can see some benefit in disposing of much of this material now, instead of holding it until it becomes obsolete, but one of the purposes of this new department should be to make this survey before the Crown Assets Corporation takes over all these materials and disposes of them recklessly. We have great aircraft factories, great ship building plants, great munitions factories. These are wonderful institutions, equipped with the most modem and up-to-date machinery. I have visited many of these factories, and I say that the production organization that has been created during the period of this war is a marvellous achievement. I have never belittled the work of the government in building up such a machine. In travelling from one end of Canada to the other with the war expenditures committee I have seen a wonderful example of industrial organization in this country. That industrial organization has been carried to the point where, if we take proper care, we can convert from war-time to peace-time production and have the greatest nation the world- has ever seen. Certainly there should be no lack of consumer goods in this country if we take the proper care. I do say, however, that if the Crown Assets Corporation carries on its work without the new Minister of Reconstruction having some control over it, we shall lose a wonderful opportunity. Instead of this great industrial expansion for which we all hope when our men and women come back from the war, by our own acts in this parliament we may put ourselves in an unfortunate position, when that could be avoided1 by the proper control.
It is true, as has been stated, that you cannot go on and produce these goods unless you have markets. Already we have some markets and we hope we may have more in future. I believe that great attention should be paid to the foreign field; yet I do not think that is the primary market for our producers. After we have properly surveyed the Whole field of domestic production and consumption-which is vital, since without proper consumption there is no use in having production-then we may turn our attention to the foreign field.
In my opinion the only time that we should be allowed to ship goods out of the country is when we have a true surplus. I do not mean just a surplus like those we had in the days of the depression. All of us remember those dreadful days, those days referred to
Department of Reconstruction

as the hungry thirties. We had an abundance of production, but the vital thing then was underconsumption. When you have that state of affairs you have a surplus of goods, but the effective demand in the hands of the people is not sufficient to buy the goods that they require. But when you have completely satisfied the home market, then you should pay attention to the foreign market. That is the only time we should look for foreign trade.
There is going to be a good field for foreign trade in those countries that have been ruined by the war. We are going to have to assist in building up those countries, but by the use of modern methods of invention and the great genius that man has to-day it will not be long before we have built them up to the point where they themselves will be looking for foreign markets. The more they get built up to the point where they themselves are looking for foreign markets, the fewer foreign markets we shall have.
I am not one of those who look forward with a great deal of pleasure to the building up of foreign credits in foreign countries. The greater the foreign credit you build up, the poorer you are going to be. It is all right to ship out surplus goods, provided that we get back goods in return. It is all right to do that if you have purchasing power in the hands of the people to buy them.
I do not underestimate the importance of foreign markets, but I think the first and most important market we must look to is our home market. We have a tremendous industry in agriculture. In his budget address to-night the Minister of Finance pointed out the possibilities of agriculture. Agriculture is one of those industries which will enable us to ship out more goods to foreign nations. If we cannot make it possible-it is not a case of being able because we can make it possible -for agriculture to produce goods and still have the cost of production plus a fair profit, then we shall be sadly lacking in our organisation under this department.
I said a moment ago that there was no use in producing abundantly unless our people have the purchasing power with which to buy. During the period of reconstruction after the war there will be a large field for employment, but if we are to continue that employment we must make sure of the income of the people. I suggest that one of the best ways of ensuring continued purchasing power for the people so that they will be able to buy the goods we produce, is the old age pension.
I think it has been generally recognized in this parliament during the last year or two

that when you give out money in the form of old age pensions you are establishing a great consumer market; you are creating a home market. We could very well lower the age limit to sixty years and increase the amount above what it is at the present time. I would suggest $50 a month. In that way we would ensure purchasing power being put into the hands of the people so that they will be able to buy the goods which industry will make.
There is no doubt that as time goes on there will be an unemployment problem with which we shall have to deal. If we can take a greater number of people out of active production by lowering the age limit for the payment of old age pensions, then we shall be solving to a degree our unemployment problem.
Then, as has been indicated, we could start at the other end and provide the young people with an educational grant sufficient to enable them* properly to fit and equip themselves intellectually to be able to assist us in our production when they come to that time of life. Here again we shall be providing purchasing power with which to buy a portion of the goods which industry can produce. We shall thus be providing a market for industry.
I believe that too much is being expected of agriculture and other secondary industries. It has been said that industry must put everybody to work, but I do not agree with that. I do not think that is the function of industry. The purpose of industry is to produce goods as cheaply as they can be produced by using the most modern methods of machinery and intellectual abilities that our organizers have. We have plenty of inventive genius. If industry could employ all the people in this country it would be a utopia; it would be wonderful, but I do not think that can be done. But everyone who is capable of working, everyone who is desirous of increasing his purchasing power, everyone who is physically and mentally fit to work should be given that privilege. Every encouragement should be given to these people to work.
The Prime Minister was speaking about this previously, and I should like to quote what he said as to how this was to be done, how we were to keep our industries in operation, how we were to put purchasing power in the hands of the people. I was very much disappointed at the answer given by the Prime Minister to a question asked by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) as to how he proposed to do this. I have marked carefully what he said because I think it holds the key to the success or failure of this new department which is to be set up.

Department oj Reconstruction
I agree with the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) when they say that we shall not be able to do this unless there is a proper and systematic and scientific change in our financial system. Apparently the Prime Minister did not agree with them. This new Department of Reconstruction null not have a chance unless it is given the power to provide the people with the necessary additional purchasing power to carry them through this reconstruction period. I am afraid that every time this new department want to do anything and they go to the treasury board, the treasury board will kick them out of the office and say, "We cannot do that because of the expense."
Look at the way in which we are treating our returned men from the last war. A minister, a member of the treasury board, makes a public statement through a i civil servant that we are not going to do anything more for the returned men from the last war, that they should abide by their contracts. No matter how sincere this minister may be, that is what will happen with this department. That is the way in which the Prime Minister said the thing would be carried on financially. The hon. member for Lethbridge asked how it would be financed and the Prime Minister said:
I will put it this way to my hon. friend. In this period of war we have been able to raise money through loans and taxation, for what purpose? For the purpose mainly of spending the money on destruction, on -the destruction of property, the destruction of community and national life, and human lives; all of which indicates that instead of having our taxes serve a useful constructive purpose, they are serving, of necessity-it is not our fault, it is the part of the penalty of war-the needs of destruction. When the whole picture is reversed, and it comes to be a matter of carrying out constructive work-
Mind you, this is the reconstruction period to which he was referring.
-work for the rebuilding of communities, for the supplying of homes, and the needs of homes, the necessaries and conveniences of life, many of which have been absolutely prohibited in the period of war, there is going to be a demand for employment the like of which has not arisen at any other time, and as one want is satisfied another want is sure to be created.
He said further:
That is the way progress is made, through demands which arise from conditions of peace and prosperity; and where you get demands of the kind which lead to the fuller employment of labour I do not think my hon. friend need fear about the increase of public debt or taxation to accomplish these things. If-
And this is the big question:
If we can get a sufficiently large demand for labour through an increasing demand for goods and commodities and things which are constructive and serviceable, I believe the nation can go ahead with the great work of construction and reconstruction and at the same time reduce its taxation and reduce its debt. That at least is what I would hope to do if this government is in office when that period comes.
These are pious hopes, hopeful platitudes, but I hardly think the Prime Minister really believes that they will bring the results for which he hopes.
We have the banking and commerce committee discussing the Bank Act and the changes that should be made in it. While I cannot prophesy what their conclusions will be, I think it is safe to say that there will be no major changes in the financial policy of this government. The Prime Minister in his speech here indicated that he hopes that this period of reconstruction will be a success, though financing it in exactly the same way that we followed before, by loans and taxation. The Minister of Finance, in his budget speech to-night, indicated that he intends to follow the same course. Yet our national debt is climbing and climbing and climbing, and while interest rates have been lowered, annual interest charges are climbing and climbing and climbing. Every loan means an additional interest charge on the incomes of the people.

I am not attempting to deal with the budget, Mr. Speaker, but when the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) was speaking he gave figures of the national debt and it was those figures I had in mind. I did not have in mind the figures given by the Minister of Finance. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, speaking on this bill, referred to the national debt. He gave the public debt of Canada as $335,000,000 in 1914 and showed that the national debt had increased by 1918 to $1,191,000,000. Then he gave what I thought was an excellent comparison. He gave the national debt in 1939, when the war started, at over 4i billion dollars. In 1943 up to December 31 the debt had risen to nearly lli billion dollars. He did not make reference to the debt as of to-day, but the Minister of Finance indicated that it had increased in the last year by about two billion dollars. At all events our public debt on December 31, 1943, was about lli billion dollars. ' In other words, it had increased about 6i times since 1914-18. The annual interest charges, according to the figures that have been put on Hansard by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, are over $304,000,000, or an interest charge for every man,
Department oj Reconstruction

woman and child in this country of over $27 per annum. That is a tremendous load to carry and the charges are continually rising, with no prospect of lowering them. Yet the Prime Minister vainly hopes that we shall be able to carry on through the reconstruction period by following exactly the same financial policies of the past. It does not take any stretch of the imagination, for anyone who sits down and analyses these figures and sees the tremendous increase which there has been from year to year ever since confederation almost, in our national debt and in the interest charges, which have increased year by year, to see that we cannot continue financing like that.
I recall the Prime Minister's great expression in 1935 when he said that if he were elected he was going to do battle with the money powers. Well, we see the results of his battle to-day, and if this is the great battle that he was going to carry on, then I have not great hopes for this reconstruction period, and I feel that the Prime Minister himself has no very great hopes in that regard either.
There must be some change in the financial policy of the government. I have already indicated two of the major steps which must be taken. Regardless of the pious hopes expressed by the Prime Minister, without some change in our financial policy there is no chance of success in the reconstruction period, nor shall we have a success made of the reconstruction department, for which we all hope, not only the minister but all of us. One of the major steps that must be taken, a step essential to the satisfactory establishment of Canadian industry to peace-time conditions is that the control of currency and credit should be removed from present private monopoly and restored to parliament and that parliament should so order the financial policy of Canada as to make available sufficient money for the financing of post-war rehabilitation and reconstruction and to ensure the consuming public of sufficient purchasing power to enable them to enjoy a standard of living limited only by the productive capacity of industry and the natural resources of the country instead of by a man-made scarcity of money.
At the present time we have a man-made scarcity of money. Without going into details of the financial reconstruction that is necessary, it seems to me that if we are to have a proper Department of Reconstruction charged with the responsibility of seeing that our country is changed over from a war-time industrial nation to a peace-time industrial

nation, we must have proper control of our currency and credit, and it must be issued in terms of public need, and not of private gain. Until we have achieved that goal I am convinced that we shall never have the success we hope for, and those who have been overseas will find, when they return home, that they have fought their fight in vain. We cannot afford that; this country cannot afford it. Therefore, let us start by putting our own house in order, getting the finances of this country on a scientific and sound basis, establishing such a financial structure that we can make financially possible anything which is physically possible and desirable. Then we shall have a Canada that our men and women overseas will be proud to return to and we shall be proud to say to them when they return: We appreciate the job which you have done, and we are going to reward you in part for all you have accomplished.

I wish to reiterate for the
information of these hon. gentlemen and others who, perhaps, think like them, that at no time have I advocated idleness. I challenge the hon. members I have named and any other hon. member now in the chamber to read my address through and pick out one sentence, one phrase, in which I advocated idleness in the post-war world. I should like to see them take up the challenge. Yet each one of these hon. members implied and, indeed, stated directly that I was advocating idleness. The type of activity to which I took exception and against which I protested was that of artificial work.
Let me give you an example of what I mean by "artificial work." In my own constituency in the so-called depression years, under tooth Liberal and Conservative administrations, roads were built with pick and shovel. Young men, some of them university graduates, were out building highways in my constituency- the Jasper-Edson highway and other roads- with pick and shovel, and machines were standing everywhere which could have been used in their place. I call that artificial work, and that is the type of work I protest against and object to. As the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) indicated in his remarks to-night, it is certainly the privilege of mankind to take advantage of all that inventive genius and productive enterprise can devise, and machinery of this kind should certainly be used to the maximum advantage. But we did not do that in the so-called depression years. It is the type of work to which we resorted then that I referred to as slavery. I did not advocate idleness; what I advocated was an opportunity for the people to put themselves to work; and if hon. members will take the trouble to read my remarks through they will find that I proposed that we so arrange our economy that all the people, instead of merely a select few, shall have an opportunity to indulge in voluntary activity.	*
Some hon. gentlemen went so far as even to bring my character into question. I hesitate to make an issue of this, but no other hon. member would take it lying down, nor do I intend to. The hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, made this statement, as reported ini Hansard, at page 4109:
Work is the fibre of achievement that makes a nation great, and you cannot have the fibre of achievement unless you have something to do and are willing to do it.
He concluded by saying this:
That is what my hon. friend lacks.
I consider that a definite questioning of my character.

I would ask the Prime Minister (Mr.'Mackenzie King), or the government as a whole, or anyone, what will happen in the event that jobs cannot be found? The whole success of reestablishment in civil life of these people, two millions or thereabouts, is to depend upon finding jobs. We know that the Liberals and the Conservatives had five years each in which to attempt to find jobs, and they were unable to do so. What is to be the condition of the people of Canada if these jobs are not forthcoming? Are wre going back to the dole, the relief line and the soup kitchen? What has the government to say with respect to this question? The hon. member for Bow River has again indicated as we in this corner
Department of Reconstruction

of the house have always insisted, that the purpose of industry is not to provide employment but to supply goods in the greatest abundance with the least amount of work and trouble. Of course the government, realizing that there will not be places in industry for all these people, are suggesting tremendous schemes of public works. When it comes to public works, is it going to be possible for the government to find jobs in public works if they are not available in industry? I happen to have on my desk a pamphlet illustrating some of the most modern machines. On the back cover is illustrated one of these huge modem dredgers, capable of lifting thirty-two tons of earth in one bite. I should like to know whether in the post-war period the government intend to permit machines of that and similar types to be used in carrying out public works of various kinds, or are they again going to do as was done before the outbreak of the war, namely, leave the machines sitting on the side of the road and put people to work with picks and shovels?
For curiosity's sake, I figured this ma'chine out on the basis of manpower-thirty-two tons of earth in one bite. If men were put to work with picks and shovels to do the work of that machine, how many men would be required? Five pounds of earth to one shovelful would be 12,000 or more shovelfuls of earth; in other words, this machine would do approximately the work of 12.000 individuals. One can go all the way through industry and public works or any other activity of man in these days and duplicate incidents of this kind. Personally, I think it is folly on the part of this government or any other government to suggest that they will be able to reestablish the members of the armed forces and others by finding jobs for them or making their entire source of income depend upon jobs that will be found either in industry or in public works.

speechtext:
This resolution anticipates the passage of a bill, the purpose of which is, in the words of the resolution, to assume the management and control of the social security and welfare of the people. I think it would be a highly desirable thing if such a department were set up to do this, if it has the power to do it. The department of health has existed for some time, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, and it will be incorporated in this new department. The department of health has not entered into the life of the people to any considerable extent. If one examines the terms of the British North America Act and looks through the twenty-nine matters which are referred to the jurisdiction of the dominion, one finds no mention

Department of National Health and Welfare
of either health or welfare. In fact, all that one does find is that quarantine and marine hospitals are put under the direction of the dominion government. It is not wonderful to me, therefore, that in these twenty-five years the department of health has existed it has not entered into or directed the life of the people. It has accomplished very little in preventing disease or preventing those mischievous actions of people who might do things deleterious to the health of the nation.
If one looks at these matters which are directed by the British North America Act to the jurisdiction of the provinces one finds several guides thereto-the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities, eleemosynary institutions other than marine hospitals. One will find property and civil rights and all matters of a purely local and private nature. So that all the nine provinces have provided themselves with departments of health or branches of welfare, and the dominion government seems to me to be assuming a very large task and perhaps an impossible one when it undertakes the management and control of the social security and welfare of the people. It does appear to me that it would be not only undesirable but harmful if this went out to the public of Canada, giving them the idea that the dominion government is able to accomplish a great deal more than in my opinion it will be able to do under this department. It is that note that I wish to sound at the very commencement of the discussion, and I call it to the attention of the Prime Minister.

Briefly I wish to say that we have no objection to the resolution passing and the bill being introduced. I should like to say, though, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), that there is a possibility that the dominion government is intruding itself into a sphere that properly belongs to the provinces. I realize, as everyone does who understands the situation confronting the Canadian economy, that there are a good many items which properly come within the jurisdiction of the provinces in which they need a good deal of assistance, in which they need that assistance from the dominion government because the dominion government is in a position to have more money than the provinces.
There is no danger involved in so far as the British North America Act is concerned if

everything that the dominion government does is designed to supplement what the provinces do. If it is definitely recognized that this is a matter of provincial jurisdiction and that the problem of the dominion is simply that of helping the provinces, then all is well. But ever since the iniquitous Rowell-Sirois report and the attempt of the government at Ottawa to jam that thing down the throats of the provinces, there has been suspicion from all over this land that the administration in Ottawa is not friendly to the British North America Act; that it is seeking to destroy the British North America Act and centralize control over the affairs of Canada in Ottawa, control that the fathers of confederation in their wisdom put in the hands of the provinces.
May I just make this suggestion, that in all these matters where the central government thinks it advisable to supplement the work of the provinces it be recognized that the provinces should take the steps and that the central government put at their disposal the means to accomplish the ends which the provinces themselves may consider ought to be accomplished, so that the dominion government does not exercise control-it may exercise administrative direction but not control. May I suggest, too, that the all-important matter in all these affairs is money. There is not a province that does not know what it wants to do with respect to health and social services if it could only find the money with which to do it. The dominion government is in a position to get that money. All the dominion government needs to do is to exercise the power which was conferred upon it by the British North America Act when it was given control over money and banking. It can make available to the provinces the money which they need. Until the men in power in Canada come to realize that, they will be faced with difficulties and do things which will endanger the Canadian commonwealth.
I have nothing more to say except to urge that the dominion government take the attitude that it will find the money with which these fine projects are to be achieved and will supply that money to the provinces in accordance with their need and then work with the provinces toward the attainment of the objectives of sound social security and social programmes in Canada. That being understood, I do not hesitate for a moment to support the resolution and the bill to be founded on it.
